blocks.text: Surrey Open Houses: streets and boundaries

items.t: This page covers public open houses across the whole City of Surrey, in the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board (FVREB) area: the board states its REALTORS® serve Surrey, Langley, White Rock, North Delta, Abbotsford and Mission, and that it supports more than 5,000 members.

Surrey open houses split into the same six City communities a touring buyer drives between — Cloverdale, Fleetwood, Guildford, Newton, South Surrey and Whalley — so a Saturday route is planned by community and by the Fraser Highway, King George Boulevard and Highway 99 corridors, not by postal code.
The signage rules on this page are Surrey's alone: they come from Surrey Sign By-law, 1999, No. 13656, a City bylaw, so the same open house run in Langley or Delta follows a different sign bylaw.

blocks.text: Surrey Open Houses: the housing stock

items.t: The stock this page shows is whatever Surrey sellers are opening that week, across the city's own housing forms: detached houses in Fleetwood and South Surrey, strata townhome clusters in Clayton and Fleetwood, and City Centre condos around King George Station in Whalley.

Townhome open houses in Surrey are usually one unit inside a single rezoned cluster — for example the RM-30 and MR4 clusters on 74 Avenue in West Clayton — so parking, visitor stalls and strata rules are set by that complex, not by the street.

Farm and acreage open houses occur on A-1 (General Agriculture) land in the Serpentine, Nicomekl and Hazelmere lowlands, where the showing includes ALR land, not just the house — see the rules section for what that changes.

blocks.text: Surrey Open Houses: rules that affect buyers

items.t: An open house directional sign needs no sign permit in Surrey, but only during the open house: Surrey Sign By-law, 1999, No. 13656 lists a "Real Estate open house directional sign for the duration of open house hours" among the signs exempt from the permit requirement.
The City's real estate sign guide tightens the timing: open house signs, including directional and A-frame signs, are only permitted on the day of an open house, during the open house hours.

On-site real estate signage is capped: the City's real estate guide states a maximum of one sign per lot frontage for a sale or rental sign, with a maximum sign area of 0.75 square metres (8 square feet) for the on-site sign along each adjacent road.

Temporary signs must come down after the event: proposed 2026 amendments to Sign By-law No. 13656, in a Council report dated June 10, 2026, restate that real estate signs and similar temporary signs displayed on any lot shall be removed by the owner within 14 days of the termination of the event identified in the sign or the completion of the sale.

Prohibited sign types apply to open house marketing too: the City's business signage page lists flashing signs (except in Special Sign Areas), roof signs, billboard signs, inflatable signs, flags as signs, painted window signs and electronic message board signs as prohibited on all properties.

The provincial rule that follows a Surrey open house is the Home Buyer Rescission Period: the BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA) states a buyer may rescind a contract to purchase residential real property up to three business days after an offer is accepted, paying the seller 0.25 percent of the purchase price, and the right cannot be waived.

blocks.text: Surrey Open Houses: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: A sign permit is required before installing permanent real estate signage in Surrey: the City's real estate sign guide states "You need a sign permit prior to installing signage" and gives the Planning and Development contact as 604-591-4370 — the exemption covers the temporary open house directional sign, not a developer's project sign.

Surrey amended its sign rules again in 2026: a Council corporate report dated June 10, 2026 proposes targeted amendments to Sign By-law, 1999, No. 13656 to improve clarity and reduce ambiguity, noting the bylaw was adopted in 1999 and has had housekeeping amendments since — a seller should check the current consolidated bylaw, not an old brokerage handout.

Deposits after an accepted offer sit in brokerage trust: BCFSA states that unless the contract says interest on a deposit is payable to the seller or the buyer, interest is payable to the Real Estate Foundation of BC — a detail most open house visitors never hear.

blocks.text: Surrey Open Houses: costs and taxes

items.t: The one fee an open house buyer can meet directly is the rescission fee: 0.25 percent of the purchase price, payable to the seller if the buyer rescinds within the three-business-day Home Buyer Rescission Period, per BCFSA.

A Surrey open house run is a driving run between six communities, anchored by transit corridors a buyer can also test on the day: City Centre in Whalley is serviced by four Expo Line SkyTrain stations ending at King George Station.

The R1 King George Boulevard RapidBus runs from Newton Exchange to Guildford Exchange through Surrey Central and King George stations, linking the two communities where weekend open houses cluster most densely in North Surrey.

The R6 Scott Road RapidBus runs from Scott Road Station to Newton Exchange along Scott Road and 72 Avenue, the route a buyer without a car would use to reach Bridgeview, Scottsdale and Newton open houses.

blocks.text: Surrey Open Houses: risks and due diligence

items.t: For a strata open house, the documents matter more than the viewing: rental-restriction bylaws are no longer allowed in BC stratas as of November 24, 2022, but short-term rental bylaws still apply and strata corporations can fine up to $1,000 a day for breaching one, per the Province's strata pages — read the bylaws before offering.

A "For Sale" sign that does not comply with Sign By-law No. 13656 is a bylaw-enforcement matter, not a title issue: the City states it is the responsibility of each business or operation to comply with the sign bylaw, and enforcement focuses first on new developments and signage already illegal under the former bylaw.

faq.q: Can a seller in Surrey leave open house signs up all week?
faq.a: No. The City's real estate sign guide states open house signs, including directional and A-frame signs, are only permitted on the day of an open house and only during the open house hours, and Surrey Sign By-law No. 13656 exempts an open house directional sign from a permit only "for the duration of open house hours." A sign standing on a Tuesday for a Saturday open house is outside both the guide and the bylaw exemption.

faq.q: If I make an offer after a Surrey open house, can I change my mind?
faq.a: Yes, within the provincial rescission window. BCFSA states the Home Buyer Rescission Period lets a buyer rescind a contract for residential real property up to three business days after acceptance, on written notice to the seller, for a fee of 0.25 percent of the purchase price. The period starts the day after acceptance is signed, and Saturdays, Sundays and holidays do not count as business days.

faq.q: Does the rescission right apply to every home I might see at a Surrey open house?
faq.a: No. BCFSA lists exemptions: residential leasehold properties, property sold at auction, and property sold under a court order or court supervision are exempt, and purchases where a disclosure statement is provided under the Real Estate Development Marketing Act carry that Act's rescission rights instead. A court-ordered sale toured at an open house in Surrey is therefore outside the three-day right.

faq.q: Who regulates the REALTOR® hosting a Surrey open house?
faq.a: The Province, through BCFSA. The local board, FVREB, is the member association for Surrey REALTORS®, not the regulator.

faq.q: Which Surrey areas can I cover in one trip?
faq.a: Group by the City's own communities — City Centre, Cloverdale, Fleetwood, Guildford, Newton, South Surrey and Whalley — which is also how the site splits its open-house pages (South Surrey and Cloverdale have their own).

faq.q: Is the host at an open house the seller's agent?
faq.a: The host is a licensee connected to the listing side of the transaction; BCFSA requires a licensee to work for either the buyer or the seller and to inform consumers of the duties owed to clients and non-clients — assume anything non-factual you tell the host can reach the seller.
